Note · Jervis — System Effects

4 min read880 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06notes/canon/canon-jervis-system-effects.md

Canon · Cluster: Systems Thinking & Complexity · Maps to Course 07 (Data & Decision-Making), E9 (Geopolitics & Macro)

  • Source: Robert Jervis, System Effects: Complexity in Political and Social Life (1997)
  • Core claim: In interconnected systems, actions produce consequences far from where they were intended — and policies designed to solve one problem routinely create others. The right posture is radical humility about second- and third-order effects.
  • Framework:
  • Interconnection means indirect effects dominate — you can't change one element without rippling the rest; the system's behavior isn't the sum of its parts.
  • Self-defeating / self-fulfilling dynamics — deterrence in one arena emboldens adversaries in another; alliances formed for security can provoke the very threat they were meant to prevent (the security dilemma).
  • The more interconnected the system, the less confident you should be about predicting any intervention's consequences.
  • Applies when: geopolitics, regulation, org-wide policy, market interventions — anywhere a "targeted fix" lives inside a dense web of reactions.
  • Breaks when: the lesson — "everything is connected, be humble" — can curdle into paralysis ("any action might backfire, so do nothing"), which is itself a choice with system effects. It's strong on why interventions surprise us, weak on what to do anyway; pair it with a bias-to-small-reversible-bets posture (canon taleb antifragile, Bezos's two-way doors canon bezos shareholder letters) so you can act and stay humble. Munger's second-order thinking is the individual-scale version (canon munger poor charlies almanack).
  • Practitioner counterpoint: (researched 2026-06-05 — r/systemsthinking corpus + Meadows/Senge transcripts) The corpus confirms Jervis's central warning and names the exact failure mode he's weak on. An r/systemsthinking thread — "Feedback appreciated: systems thinking mindset tensions" (133↑) — asks the practitioner's real question: "you're so aware the Event-level solutions don't last but Pattern-level and Structure-level solutions are much harder to achieve that you are caught between the urgent but ephemeral and the slow-burn but everlasting… How do you successfully navigate this in the Corporate world?" That's the paralysis trap rendered as a daily-work dilemma. The usable discipline stays the same: before any intervention, ask "and then what — twice" and assume the reaction you didn't model is the one that bites. Cousin to Perrow's complexity (canon perrow normal accidents).
  • Researched layer (2026-06-05)
  • Canonical explanation (sourced): the system's behavior isn't the sum of its parts, and indirect effects dominate — "a change in one area will cause ripples of change and reactions elsewhere, often in unexpected ways… feedback loops are not really loops. We have to consider the many balancing and reinforcing influences that continually affect the system" (Miles MacFarlane, The Fifth Discipline in Three Minutes). Senge's version of Jervis's humility: "the structure of the system influences the behavior more often than not… while it's easier to find someone or something to blame, the problem usually lies in how the game or system was set up in the first place" (Readitfor.me).
  • Real application (mined): the beer game / bullwhip effect is system effects you can watch happen. Four players (retailer → wholesaler → distributor → factory) each make a locally rational ordering decision "in the absence of information exchange and cooperation"; a small demand blip at the retailer amplifies into wild over- and under-ordering upstream — "supply chain delays or increases in demands can cause all kinds of havoc… which we're currently experiencing in 2021, and a little bit in 2020 with the initial pandemic with toilet paper" (Niko J). No villain, just structure: exactly Jervis's point that the consequence lands far from where the action was taken.
  • Where the corpus pushes back on the book: practitioners report Jervis's humility curdling into the paralysis he doesn't resolve — the 133↑ "mindset tensions" thread is a person stuck between knowing event-level fixes don't last and structure-level fixes being too slow. Meadows supplies the missing "what to do anyway": intervene at the highest-leverage point you can actually reach ("she lists these leverage points… least effective to most effective," paradigm shift at the top, parameter tweaks at the bottom — Ashley Hodgson), and don't waste effort on "small parameter adjustments, weak negative feedback loops" that are "way too feeble" (Global Change Management). Humility about effects, not paralysis about action.

Rep

For a change you're about to make, map two ripples: the intended first-order effect, and one second-order effect somewhere else in the system. Which actor reacts in a way you hadn't planned for?
